extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of aesthetics, visual arts (architecture, sculpture, painting) and poetry/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating and judging architecture, sculpture, painting, poetry, and drama, grounded in philosophical aesthetics and practical examples. Covers medium-specific aims (e.g., sculpture vs painting), formal devices (metre, rhyme), and conventions (allegory, historicizing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective value in architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Great wealth should be devoted to that which is objectively, i.e., actually, good and right, to what in itself is beautiful, but not to that whose value depends merely upon the association of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for styles that are intrinsically beautiful rather than those valued mainly for historical or sentimental associations. Examples: hemispherical vaults (cupola, Pantheon) give an appearance of sublimity; ancients (southern peoples) emphasized exterior supports and open-air living, while Gothic (northern) produces different interior effects. One ought not to insist on Gothic as an essential style simply from association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural form — exterior vs interior effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In antique buildings the external side is the most advantageous because there we see better the support and the burden; in the interior the flat roof always retains something depressing and prosaic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how exterior structures communicate support and burden; use forms (e.g., hemispherical cupola) that create sublimity. Architects should be aware of climatic/cultural origins of styles when choosing forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture demands beauty, strength, and fulness
rubrics_metrics.description: In sculpture beauty and grace are the principal things; sculpture demands beauty, although not always perfect, but, throughout, strength and fulness of the figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sculptural figures should avoid excessive emaciation or fragility (example: Donatello's excessively skinny John the Baptist has a repulsive effect despite masterly execution). Sculpture aims at an affirmation of the will to live; therefore the forms should convey vitality and robust completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting privileges expression, passion, and character
rubrics_metrics.description: In painting expression, passion, and character predominate; therefore just so much of the claims of beauty must be neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painting may properly present ugly or emaciated figures (example: a thin Christ upon the Cross or a dying St. Jerome) because painting can emphasize dramatic or expressive truth over perfect sculptural beauty. Painting is suited to negation of the will; it can depict suffering or decay when expressive need demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-appropriate selection of subject and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose subjects and modes of representation appropriate to the medium: sculpture for affirmation (full, strong beauty), painting for expression and negation (character, passion, the ugly when expressive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing a subject ill-suited to the medium (e.g., painting that demands sculptural idealisation, sculpture that imitates pictorial expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience necessary to realise the ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The anticipation (a priori) of the type of human beauty nevertheless requires experience by which it may be stirred up; experience assists the artist in refining the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice and frequent observation (e.g., Greeks seeing half-naked forms in gymnasia) sharpen the artist's judgment down to fine shades of difference. Poets likewise need life experience to give definiteness to their anticipatory understanding of human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation from ancient proportions as a safe aesthetic baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern sculpture that forms according to nature as it lies before it, instead of according to the proportions of the ancients, goes astray; modern architect removes himself from good taste as he departs from the style and pattern of the Greeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient (Greek/Roman) proportions and patterns are presented as the established aesthetic norm; modern artists and architects distinguish themselves mainly by wise application rather than formal invention beyond classical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical painterly skill: produce same effect by different cause
rubrics_metrics.description: A painter who understands how to separate the sensation (retinal affection) from its cause can, with technical skill, produce the same effect in the eye by an entirely different cause (patches of applied colour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The painter's craft is to recreate perceptual effects so that the beholder's understanding assigns the ordinary external cause to the painted effect. Mastery of colour, light, and patching is crucial to convincing representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture and historical painting: prefer painting from life and careful idealisation
rubrics_metrics.description: In historical paintings only portraits ought to figure, which certainly would then have to be selected with the greatest care and in some degree idealised; great artists have always gladly painted from living models and introduced many portraits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composed faces imagined wholly by the artist risk producing impossible, 'bungled' physiognomical unities; use living models or highly careful selection and idealisation when depicting specific individuals in historical scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent (subordinate) beauty in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides representing Ideas, painting has an independent beauty produced by harmony of colours, pleasing grouping, distribution of light and shade, and the tone of the whole picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These subordinate aesthetic elements (colour harmony, composition, chiaroscuro) further the viewer's state of pure knowing; treat them as valuable ornaments—analogous to diction and metre in poetry—but not as the essential end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadmissibility of allegory in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory in painting is generally inadmissible because symbolic references often fail for viewers who lack the necessary prior knowledge (e.g., kyriological hieroglyphic of Christ treading on the serpent may mean nothing to someone unfamiliar with the seed-of-the-woman motif).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allegorical devices that rely on specialized myths or doctrinal knowledge. If allegory is used, ensure symbols are sufficiently public and comprehensible to the intended audience; otherwise the image will be unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid literal depiction of non-visual phenomena (e.g., shrieking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation of shrieking in the pictorial and plastic arts (which are essentially dumb) is faulty and absurd; visual arts cannot directly represent sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an action whose salient feature is non-visual (a shriek) must be shown, represent the causal circumstances so that the lack of shrieking is plausible (example: Laocoon's contraction because the snake bites his side). Use visual substitutes or narrative context rather than literal mimicry of sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry defined: bringing the imagination into play by means of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is the art of bringing the imagination into play by means of words; the imagination of the reader is the material in which poetry exhibits its pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems should be constructed to evoke vivid mental images that the reader completes according to individuality, knowledge, and humour. One-word or small touches can be decisive; poets may spend great time to find the single right word or image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's knowledge and profundity determine poetic quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The first condition of poetry is that the poet himself has known life; according as his knowledge has been profound or superficial so will his poem be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should seek deep comprehension of human nature; excellence corresponds to correctly representing what the poet knows, and the best poets see further than their contemporaries and are often appreciated only later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific audience accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and music produce stronger, deeper, and more universal effects than plastic and pictorial arts; the latter require more culture and knowledge to prize and are often less immediately effective on common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise audience requirements: poetry and music can travel widely; visual arts may be undervalued by those without requisite cultural knowledge and can become objects of pride and rarity rather than shared feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre vs rhyme — prefer rhythm, beware rhyme's constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre (rhythm) is a nobler expedient than rhyme; metre belongs to pure sensibility (time) while rhyme is an affair of empirical sensation (hearing). Rhyme often forces violence upon thought to satisfy sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhythm as the primary formal device; guard against letting rhyme dictate thought. Rhyme is effective but can corrupt expression when sought at the expense of meaning; in some languages rhyme arose from corrupted, imperfect languages and is thus inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unforced rhymes as sign of genuine poet
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign by which one most immediately recognises the genuine poet is the unforced nature of his rhymes: they have appeared of themselves as if by divine arrangement; his thoughts come to him already in rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid visible ‘seeking’ of rhymes; the bungler seeks rhyme for the thought, the homely prosaic man seeks the rhyme for the thought, and the art is to conceal the rhyme's mechanical origin so lines do not read as merely 'boutsrimés.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme’s binary nature and avoidance of excessive accumulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhyme is from its nature binary: its effect is limited to one single recurrence of the same sound; accumulations of rhymes (third recurrence etc.) do not strengthen but create æsthetic pleonasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with forms that demand many linked rhymes (octave rhyme, terza rima, sonnet) because they often cause conflict between thought and rhyme; great poets can sometimes master them, but the forms themselves are not recommended if they lead to mental torture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: avoid poetic-only vocabulary detached from feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a disadvantage if a language has many words usable only in poetry and not in prose; such words remain foreign to our heart and exclude genuine feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer language that speaks directly to the heart; avoid an over-conventional poetic vocabulary that functions as painted sensations rather than real ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classic vs romantic poetry — prefer natural human motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between classic and romantic poetry depends on motives: the former knows only purely human, actual, and natural motives; the latter treats artificial, conventional, and imaginary motives as efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical poetry is said to have unconditional truth and correctness; romantic poetry only conditional correctness. Be wary of motifs arising from exaggerated chivalry, scholastic subtleties, or over-idealised sentimental veneration, which can distort human relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historicising/ancient scene-setting risks abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramas or poems that transfer their scene to ancient Greece or Rome often lose concreteness because our knowledge of antiquity is fragmentary, obliging the poet to avoid details and become abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive reliance on antiquity unless the poet can convincingly render details; Shakespeare is an exception who could present Greeks and Romans as contemporaneous English characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical verse may sacrifice logical connection for unity of mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent gaps or lack of logical connection in lyrical poetry are sometimes intentional to allow the unity of the fundamental sensation and mood to come through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept discontinuities when they serve a dominant affective thread—analogous to musical modulations—so long as the overall mood or fundamental sensation remains coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic construction: reveal character through escalating motives and action
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama should introduce characters in a state of peace, allow a motive to enter producing action, which elicits stronger motives and actions until passionate excitement reveals the characters' qualities and produces important actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure dramatic plots so that circumstances and events make character manifest; either character-centered or plot-centered pieces are extremes—balance is required. Great dramatists 'transform themselves into each of the persons' and voice each authentically; lesser poets tend to project themselves onto principal characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role distinctions among lyric, epic, and drama
rubrics_metrics.description: In lyrical poetry the subjective element predominates; in drama the objective element is exclusively present; epic poetry occupies a middle path combining both objective narration and subjective tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form according to aim: lyric for intimate subjective mood, drama for objective presentation of human nature and fate, epic for a balance between narrative objectivity and occasional subjectivity in tone.
